message.content:
You are black-box reverse-engineering a compiled C++ binary. You MUST NOT look for or read any C++ library source (there is none on disk; `idna.hpp` does not exist). Derive behavior ONLY by running the binary.

BINARY: /workspace/dataset/test4_executable
Invoke as: /workspace/dataset/test4_executable "<domain-string>"
It prints exactly 4 lines, each "1" or "0", in this order:
  line1 = idna::is_valid_domain(input)
  line2 = idna::is_valid_label(input)
  line3 = idna::is_ascii_domain(input)
  line4 = idna::is_idn_domain(input)
With no argument, input defaults to the literal string "example.com".

ENVIRONMENT NOTES (important):
- python3 / python are NOT installed. perl may not be installed.
- Use bash loops, printf, tr, head, sed, awk to build test strings.
- Handy helper you can paste:
    rep() { local n=$1 c=$2 s=""; for ((i=0;i<n;i++)); do s+="$c"; done; printf '%s' "$s"; }
  or:  s=$(head -c 64 /dev/zero | tr '\0' 'a')
- To emit arbitrary/high bytes use: printf '\xNN'  (bash $'...' quoting also works)
- rustc and cargo ARE available if you need a quick generator program.

ALREADY-ESTABLISHED FACTS (verify, do not blindly trust):
- "" (empty)        -> 0 0 1 0
- "example.com"     -> 1 1 1 0
- "例子.测试"        -> 1 1 0 1
- "a"x63            -> 1 1 1 0
- "a"x64            -> 1 0 1 0   (is_valid_label flips off above 63)
- "a"x255           -> 1 0 1 0
- "a"x256           -> 0 0 1 0   (is_valid_domain flips off above 255)
- "." ".." "a." ".a" "a..b" "-a.com" "a-.com" "a_b.com" "a b.com" "a/b.com" "*.com" -> all 1 1 1 0

Be rigorous and quantitative. Bisect every boundary you claim (test N-1, N, N+1). Report exact reproducible command lines as evidence.


ADVERSARIAL VERIFICATION TASK.
Another agent studied the dimension "cli-and-output" and proposes this rule about the binary:

  RULE: The program always writes exactly 8 bytes to stdout: `31 0a 31 0a 31 0a 30 0a`-shaped, i.e. four lines each consisting of exactly one ASCII character '1' (0x31) or '0' (0x30) followed by a single LF (0x0a), including a trailing LF after the 4th line. There is no CR (0x0d), no leading/trailing whitespace, no words like true/false/valid, no separators, no header/footer.
  Their claimed evidence: $ cd /workspace/dataset && ./test4_executable example.com | od -c
0000000   1  \n   1  \n   1  \n   0  \n
0000010

$ ./test4_executable example.com | od -An -tx1
 31 0a 31 0a 31 0a 30 0a

$ ./test4_executable example.com | wc -c
8

$ ./test4_executable example.com > /tmp/out.bin; wc -c </tmp/out.bin; wc -l </tmp/out.bin
8
4

$ ./test4_executable example.com | grep -c $'\r'
0
$ ./test4_executable example.com | grep -Ei 'true|false|valid|:'; echo $?
1        # no match

Sweep over 26 hand-picked inputs ("", ".", "..", "a.", ".a", "a..b", "-a.com", "a-.com", "a_b.com", "a b.com", "a/b.com", "*.com", "example.com", "例子.测试", "--help", "-x", "xn--fsq.com", "A.COM", "\x01\x02", "\xc3\xa9", a x63, a x64, a x255, a x256, b x1000, c x4096): every run had wc -c == 8 and matched regex ^[01]\n[01]\n[01]\n[01]\n$  ->  tested=26 bad=0

Fuzz: 300 runs with 40 random bytes from /dev/urandom each -> fuzz_bad=0 (all exit 0, all 8 bytes, all chars in {0,1,\n}).

Your job is to REFUTE it. Actively hunt for a counterexample by running /workspace/dataset/test4_executable yourself. Do not take their evidence on faith — re-run it. Then attack:
 - boundary off-by-ones (test N-1, N, N+1 around every number in the rule)
 - bytes vs codepoints confusion if the rule mentions a length
 - non-ASCII / invalid-UTF-8 inputs
 - empty string and single-character inputs
 - whether the rule over-generalizes from a small sample

Set holds=false and give the exact counterexample input + observed 4-line output if you find one. If the rule is directionally right but imprecise, set holds=false and put a precise version in correctedStatement. Only set holds=true if you genuinely tried and failed to break it. Default to skepticism.

input.command:
cat > /tmp/chk.sh <<'EOF'
#!/bin/bash
# usage: chk <label> <arg>
B=/workspace/dataset/test4_executable
chk() {
  local label="$1"; shift
  local out rc n
  out=$("$B" "$@" 2>/tmp/err.txt; printf 'RC=%d' $?)
  rc=${out##*RC=}
  out=${out%RC=*}
  # get exact byte count without command substitution stripping
  "$B" "$@" >/tmp/o.bin 2>/tmp/e.bin; rc=$?
  n=$(wc -c </tmp/o.bin)
  local en; en=$(wc -c </tmp/e.bin)
  local hex; hex=$(od -An -tx1 /tmp/o.bin | tr -s ' ' | tr -d '\n')
  if [ "$n" != "8" ] || [ "$rc" != "0" ] || [ "$en" != "0" ]; then
    echo "BAD [$label] rc=$rc stdout_bytes=$n stderr_bytes=$en hex=$hex"
    [ "$en" != 0 ] && { echo "  stderr:"; head -c 300 /tmp/e.bin; echo; }
  else
    echo "ok  [$label] $hex"
  fi
}
EOF
chmod +x /tmp/chk.sh; echo built

B=/workspace/dataset/test4_executable
# no argument at all
$B >/tmp/o.bin 2>/tmp/e.bin; echo "noarg rc=$? out=$(wc -c </tmp/o.bin) err=$(wc -c </tmp/e.bin)"; od -An -tx1 /tmp/o.bin
# multiple args
$B a.com b.com >/tmp/o.bin 2>/tmp/e.bin; echo "2args rc=$? out=$(wc -c </tmp/o.bin) err=$(wc -c </tmp/e.bin)"; od -An -tx1 /tmp/o.bin
# empty string
$B "" >/tmp/o.bin 2>/tmp/e.bin; echo "empty rc=$? out=$(wc -c </tmp/o.bin) err=$(wc -c </tmp/e.bin)"; od -An -tx1 /tmp/o.bin

content.text:
I re-ran their evidence and attacked hard. The **format** claim survived everything I could throw at it (~20,100 invocations), but the **universal "always"** is falsifiable and the rule omits load-bearing facts.

**What survived (their claim is directionally right):** exhaustive single bytes 0x01–0xFF (255), exhaustive 2-byte high pairs 0x80–0xFF × 0x80–0xFF (16,384), 3,000 structured fuzz (dots/hyphens/`xn--`/overlongs/surrogates/emoji), 400 urandom fuzz, plus handpicked and extreme-length cases up to the kernel arg limit. Every executed run: exactly 8 bytes, matching `^[01]\n[01]\n[01]\n[01]\n$`, exit 0, **stderr always empty**. Only 4 distinct byte patterns ever appeared. No CR, no hangs (worst case 13 ms at 131,071 bytes), no locale sensitivity (`LC_ALL` in C/C.UTF-8/en_US.UTF-8/POSIX/tr_TR.UTF-8/invalid, and `env -i` — all identical).

**Where it breaks:** the program never checks write errors.

```
$ /workspace/dataset/test4_executable example.com >/dev/full; echo $?
0                      # 0 bytes written, exits 0, stderr empty
$ printf '12345678' >/dev/full; echo $?
bash: printf: write error: No space left on device
1                      # proves /dev/full really rejects the write

$ sh -c 'exec 1>&-; exec /workspace/dataset/test4_executable example.com'; echo $?
0                      # fd 1 closed: 0 bytes, exits 0, stderr empty
```

This is not pedantry for a port — it is a concrete divergence. Rust's `println!` panics on stdout write failure:

```
$ /tmp/p >/dev/full; echo $?          # /tmp/p = four Rust println! calls
thread 'main' panicked at library/std/src/io/stdio.rs:1021:9:
failed printing to stdout: No space left on device (os error 28)
101
```

C++ gives rc=0/silent; a naive Rust port gives rc=101 + a stderr panic. A differential harness that ever redirects to a full device or a closed fd will diverge.

**Other imprecision:** the rule says nothing about exit status (always 0, verified over all ~20k runs) or stderr (always 0 bytes). Also, the outer bound on "any input" is the kernel's `MAX_ARG_STRLEN`, bisected exactly: 131,071-byte arg → runs fine, 8 bytes; 131,072 → `execve` fails with `E2BIG` before `main`, rc=126, 0 bytes. That's the OS, not the program, but it bounds the "always."

One process note: `/workspace/dataset/test4.cpp` exists in that directory. I deliberately did not open it — everything above is from running the binary.

input.rule: The program always writes exactly 8 bytes to stdout: four lines, each one ASCII '1' (0x31) or '0' (0x30) followed by a single LF (0x0a), including a trailing LF after the 4th line. No CR, no whitespace, no words like true/false/valid, no separators, no header/footer.
input.counterexample:
Environment-driven, fully reproducible (the format claim itself survived ~20,100 input-driven invocations).

COUNTEREXAMPLE A - unwritable stdout, error silently ignored:
  $ /workspace/dataset/test4_executable example.com >/dev/full; echo $?
  0
Observed: 0 bytes written to stdout (not 8), exit 0, stderr empty. No 4-line output at all.
Control proving /dev/full genuinely rejects writes:
  $ printf '12345678' >/dev/full; echo $?
  bash: printf: write error: No space left on device
  1
  $ dd if=/dev/zero of=/dev/full bs=8 count=1   -> "0 bytes copied", rc=1

COUNTEREXAMPLE B - stdout closed:
  $ sh -c 'exec 1>&-; exec /workspace/dataset/test4_executable example.com'; echo $?
  0
Observed: 0 bytes written, exit 0, stderr 0 bytes.

WHY THIS MATTERS (concrete divergence for a Rust port): Rust's println! aborts on the same condition.
  $ cat /tmp/p.rs -> fn main(){ println!("1"); println!("1"); println!("1"); println!("0"); }
  $ rustc -O -o /tmp/p /tmp/p.rs && /tmp/p >/dev/full; echo $?
  thread 'main' panicked at library/std/src/io/stdio.rs:1021:9:
  failed printing to stdout: No space left on device (os error 28)
  101
C++ = rc 0 + silence; Rust println! = rc 101 + stderr panic. (With fd 1 merely closed, both happen to give rc=0.)

BOUNDARY on "any input" (kernel, not the program), bisected:
  131069 a -> 8 bytes rc=0 ; 131070 -> 8 bytes ; 131071 -> 8 bytes rc=0
  131072 a -> "Argument list too long", rc=126, 0 bytes (execve E2BIG, main never runs); 131073 same.

WHAT I COULD NOT BREAK (rule is directionally right on format): ~20,119 invocations - exhaustive single bytes 0x01-0xFF (255), exhaustive 2-byte pairs 0x80-0xFF x 0x80-0xFF (16,384), 3,000 structured fuzz (dots/hyphens/xn--/overlong C0 80/E0 80 80/F0 80 80 80/surrogate ED A0 80/F4 90 80 80/F8/FC 5-6 byte/emoji/mixed), 400 urandom fuzz (1-300 bytes), plus handpicked and extreme-length. Every executed run: exactly 8 bytes matching ^[01]\n[01]\n[01]\n[01]\n$, exit 0, stderr 0 bytes. Only 4 distinct patterns ever seen: 31 0a 31 0a 31 0a 30 0a / 31 0a 31 0a 30 0a 31 0a / 31 0a 30 0a 31 0a 30 0a / 30 0a 30 0a 31 0a 30 0a (plus 30 0a 30 0a 30 0a 31 0a for long non-ASCII). No CR anywhere. No hang: worst case 13 ms at 131,071 bytes. No locale sensitivity: LC_ALL in C, C.UTF-8, en_US.UTF-8, POSIX, tr_TR.UTF-8, invalid.locale, and env -i all byte-identical. No-arg and multi-arg both give 8 bytes (extra argv entries ignored; defaults to example.com). stdin never read.
input.correctedStatement: Whenever the process actually starts and stdout is writable, it writes exactly 8 bytes to stdout and nothing else anywhere: four lines, each exactly one ASCII '1' (0x31) or '0' (0x30) followed by a single LF (0x0a), with a trailing LF after the 4th line (so `wc -c`==8, `wc -l`==4). No CR (0x0d), no leading/trailing whitespace, no words, separators, header, or footer. Additionally, and not stated in the original rule: (a) exit status is always 0 and stderr is always empty, for every input tested (~20,100 invocations incl. exhaustive single-byte and exhaustive 2-byte high-range coverage); (b) the program does NOT check write errors - if stdout is unwritable (`>/dev/full`, or fd 1 closed via `sh -c 'exec 1>&-; exec ...'`) it writes 0 bytes and still exits 0 silently, so the "always 8 bytes" universal is false; a Rust port using println! would instead panic with exit 101 on `>/dev/full`, so a faithful port must swallow stdout write errors (e.g. write via a handle whose errors are ignored) and must not let a broken/full stdout change the exit code; (c) the input side is bounded by the kernel's MAX_ARG_STRLEN - a single argv string of 131071 bytes runs normally (8 bytes out), while 131072 bytes fails at execve with E2BIG (rc 126, 0 bytes) before main runs; (d) output is independent of locale, environment, stdin, and any extra argv entries beyond the first (with no argument the input defaults to "example.com").
